'''''Melaleuca linariifolia''''' is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Myrtaceae]], and is endemic to eastern Australia. It is commonly known as '''snow-in-summer''', '''narrow-leaved paperbark''', '''flax-leaved paperbark''' and in the language of the [[Gadigal]] people as '''''budjur'''''. A hardy plant, it flowers prolifically in late spring or summer, making it a popular garden shrub or small tree in temperate places. ''Melaleuca trichostachya'' is a similar species but its leaves are arranged differently and the fruits have projecting [[Glossary of botanical terms|valves]].[[File:J20150602-0034—Melaleuca_linariifolia—Albany_(18470782561).jpg|thumb|225px|Street trees in [[Albany, California]]]]

==Description==
''Melaleuca linariifolia'' is a small tree growing to a height of {{convert|6-10|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} with distinctive and attractive white or creamy white, papery bark and a dense canopy. Its leaves are arranged in alternating pairs ([[Phyllotaxy|decussate]]),  [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] except when very young, {{convert|17-45|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|1-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide, linear to lance-shaped and with a distinct mid-vein.<ref name="Brophy">{{cite book |last1=Brophy |first1=Joseph J. |last2=Craven |first2=Lyndley A. |last3=Doran |first3=John C. |title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses |date=2013 |publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research |location=Canberra |isbn=978-1-922137-51-7 |pages=227–228}}</ref><ref name="Holliday">{{cite book |last1=Holliday |first1=Ivan |title=Melaleucas : a field and garden guide |date=2004 |publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers |location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W. |isbn=1-876334-98-3 |pages=174–175 |edition=2nd}}</ref>

The flowers are white to creamy-white, perfumed and arranged in spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering, sometimes also in the upper leaf axils. Each spike is up to {{convert|40|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide and long and contains 4 to 20 individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|2.5-3.3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower matures. The stamens are arranged in five bundles around the flower and each bundle contains 32 to 73 stamens. 

The flowers cover the tree over a relatively short period, between October and February and are followed by fruit which are woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]]s, {{convert|2.5-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4-5|mm|in|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} long scattered along the stems. The fruiting capsules have [[Glossary of botanical terms#V|valve]]s which do not project beyond the rim of the capsule.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="Holliday" /><ref name=Plantnet>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Peter G.|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~linariifolia|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney;PlantNet|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca linariifolia'' was first formally described in 1797 by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in ''[[Biological Journal of the Linnean Society|Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/514195|publisher=APNI|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=Smith>{{cite book|last1=Smith|first1=James Edward|title=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London: (Volume 3): Botanical Characters of Some Plants of the Natural Order of Myrti.|date=1797|location=London|page=278|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13713#page/305/mode/1up|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref> Smith noted that "This, we are told by Mr White, is a large tree, the bark of which is very thick and spongy, serving the purpose of tinder." The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''linariifolia'' means "with leaves like ''[[Linaria]]''" (a genus of plants in the family [[Plantaginaceae]]).<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="RWB">{{cite book|authorlink1=Roland W. Brown|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=340}}</ref>

==Distribution==
Snow-in-summer occurs from the [[Maryborough, Queensland|Maryborough]] district in Queensland to [[Bawley Point, New South Wales|Bawley Point]] in the [[Ulladulla, New South Wales|Ulladulla]] district in New South Wales. There is also a [[disjunction|disjunct]] population in the [[Blackdown Tableland National Park]] in Queensland. It is found in [[Heath (habitat)|heath]] and [[sclerophyll|dry sclerophyll forest]] [[habitat]]s, usually growing near watercourses or swamps.<ref name="Plantnet"/>

==Uses==
===Horticulture===
''Melaleuca linariifolia'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]] for parks and [[garden]]s and is also used as a screen or windbreak in Australia<ref name=ANPSA>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|url=http://anpsa.org.au/m-lin.html|publisher=Australian Native Plant Society, Australia|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0002165759|page=352|edition=2}}</ref> and overseas.<ref name=VT>{{cite web|title=Flaxleaf paperbark|url=http://dendro.cnre.vt.edu/dendrology/syllabus/factsheet.cfm?ID=724|publisher=Virginia Tech|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref> It is popular as a nature strip tree in [[Melbourne]] in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].<ref name="Holliday" /> It tolerates both dry and boggy conditions and is frost hardy.<ref name="Holliday" /> It should be planted with caution as it can damage wastewater pipes,<ref name=Water>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|url=https://www.sydneywater.com.au/SW/your-home/saving-water-at-home/garden-and-pool/plant-selector/plant-detail/SWP_CDF_DD_050907|publisher=Sydney Water|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref> and is easily ignitable, so should not be planted in fire-prone areas. It has also become a garden escape in Western Australia,<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|id = 19969}}</ref> it is however suitable for planting under powerlines<ref name=Yarra>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia''|url=http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/files/F30EFE63-1EDF-4954-90E6-9DA501084C40/Melaleuca_linariifolia.pdf|publisher=Yarra Ranges Shire Council|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref> and is a food or habitat sources for native animals, including many insects.<ref name="Yarra" />

There is a range of cultivars including dwarf forms such as 'Snowstorm'<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca linariifolia'' 'Snowstorm'|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/596739|publisher=APNI|accessdate=4 June 2015}}</ref> which grows to a height of {{convert|1.5|m|ft|sigfig=1}}, 'Seafoam' at {{convert|2.5|m|ft|sigfig=1}},<ref name="ANPSA" /> and 'Claret Tops' at {{convert|1.5|m|ft|sigfig=1}}, which features red coloured new growth.<ref>[http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/579 ''Melaleuca linariifolia'' 'Claret Tops']. Botanic Gardens of South Australia. Retrieved 16 February 2020</ref>

===Essential oils===
This species is rich in essential oils, especially [[Terpinen-4-ol]]. It has a wider range of tolerance to environmental conditions than the main current source of "tea tree" oil, ''[[Melaleuca alternifolia]]'' and therefore has potential as an alternative.<ref name="Brophy" />
